\chapter{At the Cooking Fire}
\label{ch:hi-at-the-cooking-fire}
\hlchaptermodality{61}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things at a Hindi cooking fire and ask for them politely.}

Complete HI-C61-stove and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bartan]{\hi{बर्तन} (bartan) — a cooking vessel}

\label{lesson:HI-C61-vessel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{mor} mean, and what did \emph{bhaĩs} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बर्तन}}
\textbf{\hi{बर्तन}} (\emph{bartan}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cooking vessel\textquotedblright{}.

\hi{बर्तन} is the word that goes with \hi{बरतना} (\emph{baratnā}), 'to handle, to make use of', and behind both stands Sanskrit \hi{वृत्} (\emph{vṛt-}), 'to turn, to carry on'. A \hi{बर्तन} is, quite literally, a thing in use.

That is why one word covers the whole shelf. A pot, a pan, a tray, a lid — each has its own name, and all of them together are \hi{बर्तन}. Ask politely for \hi{बर्तन} and you have asked for whatever the cooking needs.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things at the fire.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bartan}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bartan}, then \emph{thālī}, and say which of them is the whole shelf
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बर्तन} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a cooking vessel\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[za fa xa qa]{\hi{ज़} \hi{फ़} \hi{ख़} \hi{क़} — the same dot, a different job}

\label{lesson:HI-S141-nuqta-borrowed}



\begin{quote}
The mark from before: where does it sit, and what does it change?

On \textbf{\hi{ड}} and \textbf{\hi{ढ}} it made a flap. On these four it does something else — it lets the letter carry a sound that came into Hindi from outside it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ज़} \hi{फ़} \hi{ख़} \hi{क़}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{with the dot} & \textbf{sound} \\
\midrule
\hi{ज} & \hi{ज़} & \emph{za} \\
\hi{फ} & \hi{फ़} & \emph{fa} \\
\hi{ख} & \hi{ख़} & \emph{xa} \\
\hi{क} & \hi{क़} & \emph{qa} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{ज़}} is the \emph{z} of English \emph{zoo}. \textbf{\hi{फ़}} is the \emph{f} of \emph{far}. \textbf{\hi{ख़}} is made further back than \textbf{\hi{ख}}, at the soft palate. \textbf{\hi{क़}} is made further back than \textbf{\hi{क}}, at the very top of the throat.

Many speakers say the plain letter for all four and are understood. The dot is still printed, so a reader has to know it.

\subsection*{Script: words you already say}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{ज़रूर}} — certainly · \textbf{\hi{मेज़}} — table · \textbf{\hi{दरवाज़ा}} — door
  \item \textbf{\hi{सफ़ेद}} — white · \textbf{\hi{सफ़र}} — a journey · \textbf{\hi{तोहफ़ा}} — a gift
  \item \textbf{\hi{ख़ुशी}} — happiness · \textbf{\hi{ख़ुशबू}} — fragrance
  \item \textbf{\hi{मुलाक़ात}} — a meeting
\end{itemize}

\textbf{One pair you have met already.} \textbf{\hi{खाना}} and \textbf{\hi{ख़ाना}} were taught together, and the dot between them was named there as a fact about those two words. It is the same dot, and it is doing the same job in every word on this page. That lesson also told you the truth about it: \textbf{the dot is often left off in print}, and a reader sorts the two out from context.

\subsection*{Writing: the dotted four — copy what you see}
The letter is drawn exactly as you draw it bare. One dot goes below, clear of the line.

Put your pen on \textbf{\hi{ज़}} and follow it, then \textbf{\hi{फ़}}. Copy slowly and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and say which one means food
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{खाना}  ·  \hi{ख़ाना}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \hi{ज़रूर} and \hi{मेज़} aloud, letting the dotted letter buzz like \emph{z}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{फ़} three times, saying \emph{fa} as you finish each one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which four letters take the dot for a borrowed sound? Name the sound each one carries. What tells \textbf{\hi{खाना}} from \textbf{\hi{ख़ाना}} on the page?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chammach]{\hi{चम्मच} (chammach) — a spoon}

\label{lesson:HI-C61-spoon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bartan} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{चम्मच}}
\textbf{\hi{चम्मच}} (\emph{chammach}) — \textquotedblleft{}a spoon\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit had \hi{चमस} (\emph{camasa}), a wooden ladle lifted at sacrifices, and \hi{चम्मच} sits close enough to it that the two are often printed together. The road between them is not clean, though, so this book will show you the pair and stop there.

What is certain is the shape of the modern word: a doubled \emph{m} in the middle, and the stress landing forward. Say it twice and you will hear that it is built to be said quickly, the way the names of small everyday objects usually are.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chammach}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{chammach}, then \emph{bartan}, and say which one goes inside the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{चम्मच} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a spoon\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gilās]{\hi{गिलास} (gilās) — a tumbler}

\label{lesson:HI-C61-tumbler}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{chammach} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{गिलास}}
\textbf{\hi{गिलास}} (\emph{gilās}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tumbler\textquotedblright{}.

This one is English \emph{glass}, taken whole. It arrived with the object, the way \hi{कैमरा} arrived with the camera, and Hindi gave it a vowel in the middle so that a Hindi mouth could get through the \emph{gl-} at the front.

Watch what happened to the meaning on the way in. A Hindi \hi{गिलास} is a drinking tumbler and is very often made of steel, so the English word for the material now names an object in a language where the object is usually not made of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gilās}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{gilās}, then \emph{pānī} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{गिलास} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tumbler\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tavā]{\hi{तवा} (tavā) — a flat iron griddle}

\label{lesson:HI-C61-griddle}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{gilās} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{तवा}}
\textbf{\hi{तवा}} (\emph{tavā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flat iron griddle\textquotedblright{}.

Usually traced to a Sanskrit word on the root \hi{तप्} (\emph{tap-}), 'to heat, to burn' — the heater. The same root is inside \hi{तपस्}, the heat of hard practice, so the kitchen and the hermitage turn out to share a syllable.

A \hi{तवा} is a flat iron disc over the fire, and it is what \hi{रोटी} is made on. No \hi{तवा}, no \hi{रोटी}: the bread you met early on is defined by the surface it is cooked on as much as by the flour.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tavā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tavā}, then \emph{roṭī}, and say which one comes off the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{तवा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a flat iron griddle\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chūlhā]{\hi{चूल्हा} (chūlhā) — a cooking fire}

\label{lesson:HI-C61-stove}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{चूल्हा}}
\textbf{\hi{चूल्हा}} (\emph{chūlhā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cooking fire\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{चुल्ली} (\emph{cullī}), 'fireplace, hearth'. The oldest \hi{चूल्हा} is a horseshoe of packed clay on the floor, fed with wood at the front, with the \hi{तवा} sitting on top of it.

It also counts households. To say two brothers have separate \hi{चूल्हे} is to say they no longer eat as one family — the fire, not the roof, is what marks where one household ends. A gas ring in a city flat inherits the word and the meaning both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{बर्तन}, \hi{चम्मच}, \hi{गिलास}, \hi{तवा}, \hi{चूल्हा}. Enough to ask for what the cooking needs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chūlhā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{kṛpayā} in front of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{चूल्हा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a cooking fire\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
